line: Jumped in the game, niggas act like they coaching me
vault_lines: Jumped in the game, niggas act like they coaching me
meaning:
By saying he “jumped in the game”, 21 Savage is making a reference to how an athlete might partake in a sporting event; it’s a sports phrase that means “to join an event at full speed”, which is how 21 Savage sees his rap career.

21 started rapping in 2013 following the death of a close friend via gunshot on his 21st birthday (which served as inspiration for his rap name), thus exemplifying how he was already living the life that he raps about the moment he started: violence, shootouts, and hustling. In this way, his claims of having “jumped in the game” are justified, as he started rapping when he was already living the life he raps about at full speed.

When he states that other people “act like they coach” him, 21 Savage is basically saying that others are trying to take credit for his work. The coach of a sports team is almost always viewed as the team’s leader and motivator, but 21 is telling his listeners here that HE was the only one supporting and pushing forward his rap career, even if other people claim to have been responsible for his success in one way or another.

Additionally, 21 makes a different sports reference here to get his point across: arguably the most famous athlete in American sports history is 1990s NBA star Michael Jordan, who’s frequently called by his nickname, “Jumpman”. By saying that he “Jumped in the game”, 21 is comparing himself to Jordan here, implying that his rap career carries the same legacy as Jordan’s basketball career: one of the best to ever do it.

line: I know I can’t afford to stop for one moment That it’s too soon to for—
vault_lines: I know I can't afford to stop for one moment
meaning:
The sample that is prominently featured throughout the entirety of the first part is taken from Aretha Franklin’s 1965 single “One Step Ahead:” in this case, two lines from different parts of the song are spliced and edited to be side to side.

The first line is taken from Aretha’s second verse, whereas the second line comes from the bridge: these latter words are also cut off, causing the sample to sound like “too soon, too far,” when in reality it’s “too soon, to for-get you”.

While Aretha was one step ahead from being heartbroken, JID is one step ahead of the competition in the rap game, which he compares to being one step ahead of the competition in dealing drugs.

Franklin’s lyrics were similarly restructured on the chorus of Mos Def/Yasiin Bey’s 1999 song “Ms. Fat Booty,” a song JID pays homage to here.
